html:
The Houma are a Native American people of the lower Mississippi, in what is now Mississippi and Louisiana. They spoke a Muskogean language close to Choctaw. Their name means "red", and the red crawfish was their emblem.

When French explorers came down the river, La Salle in 1682 and Iberville in 1699, the Houma lived on the east bank of the Mississippi near the mouth of the Red River. A red pole marked the edge of the hunting grounds between them and the Bayogoula to the south; the French called the spot Baton Rouge, "red stick", and the city kept the name. The Houma farmed maize and hunted.

Disease and war pushed them south. In 1706 the Tunica, who had come to live with them, turned on them and killed many. The Houma moved down the river toward New Orleans, and later into the bayous of southern Louisiana, where they fished, trapped and farmed, and the town of Houma is named after them. Today the United Houma Nation has many thousands of members but no federal recognition. Their neighbours included the Natchez and the French of Louisiana.
